Architecture Diagram

This single-project photo gallery serves a server-rendered web interface and uses Azure Blob Storage for image persistence. There is no relational database or separately deployed application service.

Data Storage & External Services

Azure Blob Storage is the only application persistence service. The application lists block blobs, uploads objects, and deletes them; there is no database, cache, or message broker. The container is created with public blob-read access, so browsers can load the resulting blob URLs directly.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • A single MVC controller combines request handling and direct Blob Storage operations; no separate service or repository layer is defined.
  • Blob objects, rather than relational records, are the gallery's persistence model.
  • The container is accessed through a mutable static BlobContainerClient shared by controller requests.

Management & Observability Endpoints

No health-check, metrics, management, or API documentation endpoints were found. No custom metrics are registered.

DTOs & Contracts

No explicit request/response DTO classes, OpenAPI specification, protobuf schema, or GraphQL schema were found. The gallery action passes a List to its Razor view; uploads use the MVC Request.Files collection, and image deletion binds the name action parameter. The application has no custom JSON serialization configuration.

Communication Patterns

The browser communicates with MVC using HTTP requests and multipart form submissions. Controller actions call the Azure Blob Storage SDK directly; the SDK operations use the configured storage endpoint, with UseDevelopmentStorage=true as the checked-in default. The controller uses asynchronous SDK calls for container creation, upload, and deletion, while blob enumeration is synchronous.

No application-level retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads, service discovery, API gateway, or inter-service messaging are configured. The only route composition is conventional MVC routing. No authentication, authorization, or HTTPS-enforcement configuration was found; blob reads are explicitly public, and app-level actions do not check user identity or roles.

Core Business Workflows

The application provides a simple image gallery: users can browse stored images, upload images, remove one image, or clear the gallery. Gallery items are represented by objects in a single storage container.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
Image blobWebApp-Storage-DotNet / GalleryUser-provided image object displayed in the galleryStored in the gallery container; exposed to the browser through its blob URL
Blob containerAzure Blob Storage / Image persistenceCollection of gallery objectsContains image blobs

No application-level domain entity classes or aggregates were found.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
WebApp-Storage-DotNetPhoto GalleryGallery operations and image referencesAzure Blob Storage
Azure Blob StorageImage persistenceStored image blobsNone identified

There are no additional services, bounded contexts, or cross-context data exchanges.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse the Gallery

  1. A visitor opens the default gallery page.
  2. HomeController.Index creates the configured container if needed and lists block blobs.
  3. The controller passes blob URIs to the gallery view.
  4. The browser loads each image directly from its public blob URL.

The workflow has no application-level sign-in, authorization, or per-image access check.

Workflow 2: Upload Images

  1. A visitor selects one or more files and submits the multipart form.
  2. HomeController.UploadAsync iterates over the submitted files and creates a generated blob name using the original extension.
  3. The controller sends the posted filename string to the Blob Storage SDK as the upload source path, then redirects to the gallery after successful processing.
  4. If a storage operation throws an exception, the controller returns the error view.

No business validation for file type, content, or file count is present.

Workflow 3: Delete Images

The single-image action accepts a URI string, extracts its final path segment as the blob name, and deletes that object if present. The delete-all action enumerates the container and deletes each block blob. Both actions redirect to the gallery on success and display an error view on failure.

Cross-Service Data Flows

The application communicates only with Azure Blob Storage. The controller lists blob names and URIs for display, performs uploads and deletions, and the browser reads image content from public blob URLs. No aggregation across application services or fallback data source is implemented; storage failures yield an error view.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant Visitor participant Gallery as "Gallery Web Application" participant Storage as "Azure Blob Storage" Visitor->>Gallery: Select images and submit Gallery->>Gallery: Generate blob names from timestamps, identifiers, and extensions Gallery->>Storage: Upload each submitted file alt Storage accepts the uploads Storage-->>Gallery: Upload operation completes Gallery-->>Visitor: Redirect to gallery Visitor->>Gallery: Browse gallery Gallery->>Storage: List block blobs Storage-->>Gallery: Blob URLs Gallery-->>Visitor: Render gallery Visitor->>Storage: Read public image URL Storage-->>Visitor: Image content else Storage operation fails Storage-->>Gallery: Operation exception Gallery-->>Visitor: Render error view end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • The gallery displays only block blobs returned from the configured container.
  • Uploaded blob names are generated from the current timestamp, a GUID, and the original file extension.
  • A single-image deletion derives the blob name from the supplied URI; delete-all targets block blobs in the container.
  • No upload-type, content, or count validation is implemented.
  • No transaction, application-level audit trail, or business authorization rule was identified.
  • Controller exceptions are returned to the error view with message and stack trace values.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The package set contains multiple known vulnerable versions: Microsoft.Data.OData 5.6.4, jQuery Validation 1.11.1, Newtonsoft.Json 6.0.8, Bootstrap 3.0.0, jQuery 1.10.2, and Azure.Storage.Blobs 12.9.1. The separate advisory report records the applicable GitHub Security Advisories and patched versions. The project targets .NET Framework 4.8 and uses legacy non-SDK project infrastructure, which limits modern cross-platform build and upgrade tooling.

Notable Observations

  • Dependency resolution could not run because Microsoft.WebApplication.targets is unavailable in the Linux environment; transitive dependency coverage is therefore incomplete.
  • The app's storage behavior is built around Azure Blob Storage rather than a relational database or ORM.
  • No test-scoped package dependencies are declared.
  • The project references both Newtonsoft.Json and System.Text.Json packages.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The application has no relational entities or ORM model; its gallery data consists of image blobs in one Azure Blob Storage container. Blob names and URLs are used by the controller and view as the application's only persisted references.

Caching Strategy

No application cache, cache provider, cache-aside pattern, or query-result cache was identified. The mutable static container client is a shared SDK reference, not a data cache.

Data Ownership Boundaries

There is one application and one external blob container, with no cross-service data access, shared relational database, or CQRS pattern. HomeController directly lists, uploads, and deletes blobs; the browser receives blob URLs and reads publicly accessible objects directly from storage. No separate source-of-truth boundary exists across application services.
